title: Deduplicate on the full content
statement: Deduplicate and count items on their full content, not on an opening prefix or an earlier step's count.
example: Hashing only the first 200 characters wrongly marked 34% of distinct records as duplicates.
detail: A training-set build hashed the first 200 characters of each record, so different records that open alike, such as multiple-choice items with the same question opening, counted as duplicates: it seemed to hold 37k unique records, a 34% false duplicate rate, until full-content hashing found 56,554 in one source file alone (`training_data_70k.md`, lines 30-33). A source pool reported as about 31 candidates per objective held 12-14 unique documents once deduplicated, because the reported count included repeats across rounds (`feedback_cache_pool_count_vs_unique_doc_count_distinct_2026_06_01.md`, lines 7-9).
against: A whole-item hash catches only exact copies; near-duplicates need another test, and the folder has none.

evidence.quote: `build_70k_dataset.py` used MD5 hash of first 200 chars of assistant content for dedup. This caused massive FALSE POSITIVES — many different records share the same first 200 chars (e.g., MCQs with the same question opening). Fixed to use **full content MD5 hash**.
**Before fix:** appeared to have only 37k unique records (34% false dedup rate)
Actual unique-doc pool was 12-14 per KC after dedup, not 31.
**Bug:** Used MD5 hash of first 200 chars of assistant content for deduplication.

This caused massive FALSE POSITIVES. Many different records share the same opening 200 characters:
- MCQs starting with "Which of the following best describes..."
- LEQs starting with "Evaluate the extent to which..."
- DBQs starting with "Using the documents..."

Result: Appeared to have only 37k unique records from what should have been 59k+. A 34% false dedup rate made the dataset look much smaller than it was, and caused us to think we needed to generate more data.
**Fix:** Full content MD5 hash of the entire assistant response.
**After fix:** 56,554 from raft_combined alone were correctly unique. We didn't need to generate anything.
Row identifiers, wrappers, scores, metadata, and difficulty labels do not create a new candidate identity. This prevents repeated packaging or rescoring from inflating the unique count.
